cases.answer: My strength is staying methodical when things move fast, and the clearest example was a night shift on a surgical ward. A man in his sixties, two days after bowel surgery, became pale and breathless, with six beds under my care that night. I was the nurse responsible for him, and the delay of even an hour could have meant intensive care. I checked his observations, sat him upright, started oxygen, then rang the surgical registrar. He was stable within 30 minutes and stayed on the ward, which spared him a transfer to the high dependency unit. What I took from it is that a fixed routine under pressure frees me to think clearly.

During a placement on an acute medical unit last winter, an older woman admitted with a chest infection was in my care. Her breathing had been slowly worsening through the afternoon and the early warning score was creeping up. I was the nurse assigned to her, and her full assessment that shift was my responsibility. I measured her respiratory rate, examined her chest, questioned her on pain, then charted everything. The score showed she was deteriorating, so the doctor reviewed her within twenty minutes and her antibiotics were changed. Her oxygen saturation rose from 89 to 95 per cent by the evening. I learned that a thorough assessment tells you more than the numbers alone.

On a busy afternoon shift on a care of the elderly ward, a patient's blood pressure ended up recorded from the arm with the drip in, and the reading, far too low to be right, went on the chart unchallenged. The mistake was mine, and he was already feeling unwell, so a missed deterioration could have harmed him. The nurse in charge was told that same afternoon and an incident report went in before handover, because owning the error openly, whatever it cost me, was my line from the first minute. I retook his blood pressure, corrected the chart, then taped up a reminder. His true reading was low but not dangerous, and the doctor adjusted his fluids within the hour, so no harm came to him. Our observation form now has a box for the arm used, and similar entries fell to zero over the next three months. The lesson for me is that a reading that doesn't fit the patient deserves a second look.

The hardest situation I have faced was a night shift on an acute admissions unit, when a young man came in with abdominal pain that the first assessment had put down to a stomach bug. By 3 a.m. his pain was worse and his heart rate was climbing, and a missed surgical emergency would have been serious. I was the nurse responsible for his observations and for deciding when to escalate. I reassessed his abdomen, repeated his observations, then paged the surgical registrar. He went to theatre within the hour with an inflamed appendix and recovered without complications. Everyone on the unit now gets a reassessment when pain changes, which cut missed escalations to none that quarter. What I took from it is to trust a changing pattern over the first label.

I checked his blood glucose, gave fast-acting sugar by mouth, then called the diabetes team. His glucose climbed back to a safe range within twenty minutes and he avoided a seizure or an admission to intensive care. The diabetes team changed his dose, and he went home on schedule. I learned that acting on the first signs is better than waiting for the next round.
